Mount & Blade: Warband Review

Audio: 9/10 - pretty good soundtrack

Balance: 7/10 - mostly fine but very late-game is pretty difficult

Design: 7/10 - pretty easy to understand but some features and mechanics could be better explained in game

Fun: 10/10 - wars, sieges, raids, battles, what more can be said?

Gameplay: 9/10 - good blend of strategic map conquest and first-person battles

Graphics: 6/10 - pretty old and outdated now, but impressive for the time

Extras: 10/10 - extensive modpacks (specifically Floris) make this game worth playing years after its release

Playtime: 9/10 - long playtime, but you might want to try this game’s sequel, Bannerlord, eventually

Stability: 9/10 - no major issues

Story: 6/10 - would be nice if there was better developed lore and story, but it's not necessary

Total: 82 sea raider’s skull cups out of 100

This is an RPG in its purest form. You start out as a nobody, and everything else is up to you. This game is truly open to you and whatever you want to do. You can do anything from becoming a lone adventurer, all the way to king of the land. You can swear allegience to a nation and become part of the army, or form your own band of bandits/mercenaries and be the scourge of the land. You can form your own nation through war, or help a claiment overthrow and re-establish a nation. And so much more.

Add in mods and you got yourself the deepest, most open RPG released in the past decade.
Such an amazing game, that still is wonderful to play even 14ish years after its release.

My dream medieval RPG, would be a world like Oblivion, an engine like Source or iD Tech, and the combat system featured in this game. It doesn't matter how big your sword is, it's all in how you use it. With damage being dealt primarily through relative speed, new characters can still make a significant impact in any battle, while the oldest and richest of characters can still fall prey to roving bandits, if they're not careful.

The demo provides full, unrestricted access to the game world and its content, coming only with a level 7 cap on characters which you may continue to play after purchasing the game. There's no reason not to try it out.

You can get some unique quests or you can just assist a kingdom to build yourself up and earn a fief in service of them. Honestly it's the easier path. It's still repetitive though.

Game with both very strong single player and multiplayer scenes.

Singleplayer

Long, fun and rewarding sandbox campaign where you can do or become whatever you want. Be a man of the people, help the little guys and purge brigands from their lands. Maybe sell your sword and sign your warband as mercenaries in service of one of the major kingdoms. Build up your renown and become a loyal vassal, and be awarded land. Build an anarcho-capitalist empire owning dyeworks, ironworks, and weaveries all over the land while enforcing the NAP on those pesky viking raiders with your Recreational Swadian Knights™

Multiplayer

Skill based matches in a variety of gamemodes including TDM, DM, seige and duel. Very large servers, sometimes upto 200 players. Napoleonic Wars DLC is where it shines, though, as there is a large and active community, aswell as community made regiments that participate in huge organized battles. Some are serious, others are more laid back and play for fun.

To conclude, Mount and Blade: Warband has a great amount of content and replayability for it's price. I'd recomend picking it up, even before Bannerlord (Warband 2) is announced to get a taste of what it will be like.

First things first, this game's visuals are bad, especially when you consider that games like Xenoblade Chronicles and Mass Effect 2 came out this same year.

However, TaleWorlds cracked the code on a core gameplay loop that is simultaneously so addictive in its reward structure and soothing in its consistency that I can only refer to it as Medieval Animal Crossing. The combination of real-time combat, RPG mechanics, and wargaming elements works so organically and gives you a way to always be making progress.

As your warband grows stronger and your lord/lady increases in reputation, M&B:W becomes less of an action RPG and more of a strategy game. The friends and enemies you make in the world as a mere mercenary or vassal become crucial in making or breaking your empire should you try to seize the throne. Your "companions" make up a JRPG-esque party that levels up as they fight alongside you, and they can eventually become your vassals and generals in your army. This game has no "story", but the narrative of your character and his/her struggles will start to form spontaneously as you move through the world, creating really organic and compelling moments of failure, betrayal, and triumph.

Verdict: This game is like crack, and every year I find myself coming back to spend another 20+ hours in Calradia.
